condition: \text{a recipe uses } 2 \text{ cups of flour for every } 3 \text{ eggs}
shortcut_explanation: 9 eggs is 3 times as many as 3 eggs. So you need 3 times the flour: 3 × 2 = 6 cups.
full_explanation: The recipe keeps the same ratio. 3 eggs need 2 cups, and 9 eggs is three groups of 3 eggs. Three groups of 2 cups make 6 cups. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: Move 2 from 37 over to 48. Then 48 + 37 becomes 50 + 35.
full_explanation: Taking 2 from one number and giving it to the other doesn't change the total. 48 + 2 = 50 and 37 − 2 = 35. Both sums are 85. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left, so 3.5 becomes 35. Dividing by 100 moves each digit two places to the right, so 350 becomes 3.5.
full_explanation: 3.5 × 10 = 35. 350 ÷ 100 = 3.5. 35 is ten times as big as 3.5. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

quantity_a: \text{one angle of a triangle whose three angles are equal}
shortcut_explanation: A triangle's angles add up to 180°, so each equal angle is 60°. Half of a right angle is 45°.
full_explanation: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. Three equal angles share it, so each one is 180 ÷ 3 = 60. A right angle is 90 degrees, and half of it is 45. 60 is more than 45. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: 25% is the same as a quarter. Both take a part of the same 60, and a third is a bigger part than a quarter.
full_explanation: A third of 60 is 20. 25% is ¼, and a quarter of 60 is 15. Cutting 60 into 3 pieces gives bigger pieces than cutting it into 4. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

quantity_a: \text{the smallest number that both } 4 \text{ and } 6 \text{ go into}
shortcut_explanation: Count in 6s and stop at the first number 4 goes into: 6, 12. It's 12, not 4 × 6.
full_explanation: Counting in 6s gives 6, 12, 18, 24 and so on. 4 goes into 12, because 4 × 3 = 12. That makes 12 the smallest one, and 12 is less than 24. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.
√49 asks which number times itself makes 49. That number is 7. 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. 8 is more than 7. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

quantity_a: \text{the area of a square with perimeter } 20
shortcut_explanation: Perimeter 20 means each of the 4 sides is 5. The area is 5 × 5 = 25.
full_explanation: A square has 4 equal sides, so each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5. The area is side times side: 5 × 5 = 25. 25 is more than 20. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Test 0 as well as other numbers. 0² = 0 is a tie, but 1² = 1 wins.
full_explanation: A square is never negative, because a negative times a negative is positive. If x = 0, both sides are 0. If x = 1, x² = 1 is more than 0. Two different results mean you can't tell. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: 0.1 is one tenth. Taking a tenth of a number is the same as dividing it by 10.
full_explanation: Try x = 30: 30 ÷ 10 = 3, and 30 × 0.1 = 3. Multiplying by 0.1 takes one tenth, and dividing by 10 splits it into ten equal parts and keeps one of them. This works for every number, even 0 and negatives. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: 20% of 60 is 12. Take it away: 60 − 12 = 48.
full_explanation: 10% of 60 is 6, so 20% is 12. A discount takes that off the price: 60 − 12 = 48. 48 is less than 50. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: The average sits halfway between x and 10. Try x = 0, then x = 20.
full_explanation: If x = 0, the average is 5, which is more than 0. If x = 20, the average is 15, which is less than 20. The average is always between the two numbers, so it depends on whether x is below 10 or above 10. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: √9 = 3 and √4 = 2, so A is 3 × 2 = 6. √36 is also 6.
full_explanation: 3 × 3 = 9, so √9 = 3. 2 × 2 = 4, so √4 = 2. 3 × 2 = 6, and 6 × 6 = 36, so √36 = 6 too. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: A fraction bar works like brackets around the top. So A is 10 ÷ 2 = 5, but B is 6 + 2 = 8.
full_explanation: In A, the whole top 6 + 4 = 10 is split in half, which gives 5. In B, only the 4 is split in half, which gives 2, and then 6 is added: 8. 8 is more than 5. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: −x is not always negative. Try x = 1, then x = −1.
full_explanation: If x = 1, then −x = −1, and 1 is more. If x = −1, then −x = 1, and now B is more. The minus sign flips a number to the other side of 0. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: Adding y only makes x bigger when y is positive. Try y = 1, then y = −1.
full_explanation: If x = 1 and y = 1, then x + y = 2, which is more than 1. If x = 1 and y = −1, then x + y = 0, which is less than 1. Adding a negative number makes a total smaller. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: 10³ = 1000. Keep multiplying by 3: 3, 9, 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187. You pass 1000 before you use all ten 3s.
full_explanation: 10³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. For 3¹⁰, keep multiplying by 3: 9, 27, 81, 243, 729, and then 2187 at the seventh 3. That is already past 1000, and there are three more 3s to go. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: 10 pens is 4 pens, 4 more pens and 2 more. 2 pens are half of 4, so they cost 3: 6 + 6 + 3 = 15.
full_explanation: 4 pens cost 6, so 2 pens cost half as much, which is 3. 10 pens is 4 + 4 + 2 pens. That costs 6 + 6 + 3 = 15. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: An even power hides the sign. x could be 3 or −3: both squares are 9, which is more than 4.
full_explanation: If x = 3, then x² = 9 is more than 4, and x is more than 0. If x = −3, then x² = 9 too, but x is less than 0. Squaring can't tell you if x was negative. So the answer is D: not enough information.

quantity_a: \text{the area of a rectangle } x \text{ by } 2x
quantity_b: \text{the area of a square with side } x
shortcut_explanation: The rectangle is two of those squares side by side. Try x = 3: 18 and 9.
full_explanation: The rectangle's area is x × 2x, which is 2 lots of x × x. The square's area is just x × x. With x positive, double the area is bigger, for every x. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Test a small fraction and one close to 1. Try x = 0.1, then x = 0.9.
full_explanation: If x = 0.1, half of it is 0.05, but 0.1² = 0.01, so A wins. If x = 0.9, half of it is 0.45, but 0.9² = 0.81, so B wins. Two different results mean you can't tell. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: 10% of x is exactly 10 only when x is 100. Try a big x and a small x.
full_explanation: If x = 200, 10% of 200 is 20, so A is 220 and B is 210. If x = 50, 10% of 50 is 5, so A is 55 and B is 60. Bigger numbers get a bigger 10%. So the answer is D: not enough information.

condition: \text{four numbers have an average of } 10, \text{ and a fifth number } x \text{ is added, with } x > 10
shortcut_explanation: A new number above the average pulls the average up.
full_explanation: Four numbers with an average of 10 add up to 40. Adding x makes the total 40 + x, shared among 5 numbers. Try x = 15: 55 ÷ 5 = 11. Any x above 10 lifts the average above 10. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

condition: n \text{ is a whole number from } 1 \text{ to } 10
shortcut_explanation: 5 × 5 = 25 ends in 5, and so does 25 × 5 = 125. Multiplying a number that ends in 5 by 5 always ends in 5 again.
full_explanation: 5¹ = 5, 5² = 25 and 5³ = 125. Each time, you multiply a number ending in 5 by 5. The last digit then comes from 5 × 5 = 25, which ends in 5. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: x is 2 parts and y is 3 parts, so x is 2 of the 5 parts. 2/5 is less than a half.
full_explanation: Split everything into equal parts: x is 2 parts and y is 3 parts. Together they make 5 parts, and x is 2 of them. That makes the fraction 2/5, and 2/5 is less than 2.5/5, which is a half. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: 0.99x is 99 hundredths of x, a little less than all of x. Try x = 100: 100 and 99.
full_explanation: Multiplying a positive number by something less than 1 makes it smaller. 0.99 is just under 1, so 0.99x is just under x. Try x = 100: 0.99 × 100 = 99, which is less than 100. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: The 3 outside the brackets multiplies both x and 2. So B is 3x + 6.
full_explanation: 3(x + 2) means three lots of x + 2: x + 2 + x + 2 + x + 2, which is 3x + 6. A is 3x + 2. Both have the same 3x, and 6 is more than 2, for every x. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Add the smallest values: more than 4 plus more than 6 is more than 10.
full_explanation: x is more than 4 and y is more than 6. Adding them, x + y is more than 4 + 6 = 10. Try x = 5 and y = 7: 12. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: x doesn't have to be a whole number. Try x = 1, then x = ¼.
full_explanation: If x = 1, then 2x = 2, which is more than 1. If x = ¼, then 2x = ½, which is less than 1. Unless it says whole number, test a fraction. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: Two n's make 2n, and the extra 1 makes 2n + 1.
full_explanation: Try n = 7: 7 + 8 = 15, and 2 × 7 + 1 = 15. In general, n + (n + 1) has two n's and one 1. That is 2n + 1 for every n. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: A third is two sixths. Two sixths plus one sixth is three sixths, which is a half.
full_explanation: x/3 is the same as 2x/6. Add x/6 and you get 3x/6. Three sixths is one half, so both sides are x/2 for every x. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: Try x = 9: √9 = 3, but 9 − 2 = 7. Once x is past 4, x − 2 grows much faster than √x.
full_explanation: Let r stand for √x, so x = r × r, and r is more than 2 because x is more than 4. Then r × r is more than 2 × r. That makes x − 2 more than 2r − 2, which is r + (r − 2), and that is more than r. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Between 0 and 1, powers make a number smaller and square roots make it bigger. Try x = ¼: x³ = 1/64 and √x = ½.
full_explanation: Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes things smaller, so x³ is less than x. The square root of a number between 0 and 1 is bigger than the number, like √¼ = ½. That puts x³ below x and √x above x. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: A percent of a percent multiplies: 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06, which is 6%.
full_explanation: Try x = 1000: 30% of 1000 is 300, and 20% of 300 is 60. 6% of 1000 is also 60. Taking 20% of 30% is 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06 of x, every time. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

quantity_a: \text{the remainder when } n \text{ is divided by } 4
shortcut_explanation: Even numbers can leave a remainder of 0 or 2 when you divide by 4. Try n = 2, then n = 4.
full_explanation: If n = 2, then 2 ÷ 4 is 0 with 2 left over, so the remainder is 2. If n = 4, it divides exactly, so the remainder is 0. Being even doesn't tell you which. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: x² is the same as |x| × |x|. Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes it smaller.
full_explanation: |x| is the distance of x from 0, which here is between 0 and 1. x² is |x| × |x|, and multiplying by a number less than 1 shrinks it. Try x = −½: |x| = ½, but x² = ¼. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Think in parts: a is 1 part, b is 2 parts and c is 3 parts. 1 + 2 = 3, so a + b matches c.
full_explanation: Each part is the same size, so a + b is 1 + 2 = 3 parts. c is also 3 parts. Try a = 5: then b = 10 and c = 15, and 5 + 10 = 15. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

condition: x \text{ is the biggest angle of a triangle, and its three angles are all different}
shortcut_explanation: The three angles share 180°, so they average 60°. The biggest of three different angles must be above the average.
full_explanation: The three angles add up to 180 degrees. If the biggest angle were 60 or less, all three would be 60 or less. Then they could only reach 180 if each one were exactly 60, but the angles are all different. That means the biggest angle is more than 60. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Two of the same number is 2 times that number. 2 × 2²⁰ is 2²¹.
full_explanation: Adding a number to itself doubles it. Doubling 2²⁰ adds one more 2 to the multiplication, which makes 2²¹. Watch out: it is not 2⁴⁰, which would be 2²⁰ times 2²⁰. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: Multiplying by more than 1 makes positive numbers bigger, but negative numbers smaller. Try x = 2, then x = −2.
full_explanation: Take y = 2. If x = 2, then xy = 4, which is more than 2. If x = −2, then xy = −4, which is less than −2. Stretching a negative number moves it further below 0. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: Don't only test whole numbers. Try a = b = 3, then a = b = 1.5.
full_explanation: If a = b = 3, then ab = 9 and a + b = 6, so A wins. If a = b = 1.5, then ab = 2.25 and a + b = 3, so B wins. Numbers just above 1 barely grow when you multiply them. So the answer is D: not enough information.

condition: \text{a triangle has sides } x, y \text{ and } 10

domain.y: real, y > 0, x + y > 10, abs(x - y) < 10

shortcut_explanation: In any triangle, two sides together are longer than the third side.
full_explanation: Picture walking along sides x and y instead of straight along side 10. The straight path is always the shortest, which is why x + y is more than 10. If x + y were 10 or less, the two short sides couldn't meet to close the triangle. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: A − B is (x − 1)², which is 0 at x = 1 and positive for every other x. So A never loses, but it can tie.
full_explanation: Try x = 2: 5 and 4, so A wins. Try x = 1: 2 and 2, a tie. A − B is x² − 2x + 1 = (x − 1)², a square, so B never wins. A sometimes wins and sometimes ties, so you can't tell. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: x³ > x² only works when x is more than 1. For a positive x, |x| = x.
full_explanation: If x is 0 or negative, x³ is 0 or negative, but x² is 0 or positive, so x³ can't be bigger. If x is between 0 and 1, x³ is smaller than x². That leaves only x more than 1, and then |x| = x. So the answer is C: the two quantities are equal.

shortcut_explanation: A bigger percent can beat a bigger starting number, or it can lose. Try a = 10, b = 11, then a = 1, b = 2.
full_explanation: If a = 10 and b = 11, A is 15 and B is 13.2, so A wins. If a = 1 and b = 2, A is 1.5 and B is 2.4, so B wins. It depends on how close a and b are. So the answer is D: not enough information.

condition: n \text{ and } n + 2 \text{ are both prime numbers}
shortcut_explanation: Look for pairs of primes that are 2 apart: 3 and 5, then 5 and 7. So n could be 3 or 5.
full_explanation: If n = 3, then n + 2 = 5, and both are prime, so A and B tie. If n = 5, then n + 2 = 7, also both prime, and 5 is more than 3. So the answer is D: not enough information.

shortcut_explanation: Each power of 0.1 makes the number ten times smaller. 0.1² = 0.01, so a higher power is smaller.
full_explanation: 0.1² = 0.01 and 0.1³ = 0.001. Raising a number between 0 and 1 to a higher power makes it smaller, even for powers like 2.5. That means 0.1ˣ is less than 0.01 for every x above 2. So the answer is B: Quantity B is greater.

shortcut_explanation: Try x = 2: 2 + ½ = 2½. Try x = ½: ½ + 2 = 2½ again. Only x = 1 gives exactly 2.
full_explanation: x + 1/x − 2 is the same as (x − 1)² ÷ x. With x positive, that is a square divided by a positive number. It is 0 only at x = 1, so here A is always more. So the answer is A: Quantity A is greater.

shortcut_explanation: x² > y² only says x is further from 0 than y is. x could be 3 or −3.
full_explanation: If x = 3 and y = 1, A is 2 and B is −2, so A wins. If x = −3 and y = 1, A is −4 and B is 4, so B wins. Squares hide the sign of x. So the answer is D: not enough information.

quantity_a: \text{the average of } a, b \text{ and } c
shortcut_explanation: The average is the middle number only when the numbers are evenly spaced. Try 1, 2, 3, then 1, 2, 9.
full_explanation: With 1, 2 and 3, the average is 6 ÷ 3 = 2, the same as b. With 1, 2 and 9, the average is 12 ÷ 3 = 4, which is more than b. A far-away number pulls the average toward it. So the answer is D: not enough information.
